args.summary: 65M with MRSA bacteremia and infective endocarditis on IV antibiotics developed new chest pain, then rapid hemodynamic deterioration into cardiogenic shock. Echo shows new LV regional wall-motion abnormalities and a pericardial effusion that progressed to tamponade. ECG and vitals details are not available in the source. The combination fits an acute coronary event from septic embolism, possibly complicated by rupture or hemopericardium. Another possibility is a perivalvular abscess or pseudoaneurysm eroding into the pericardium or a coronary artery, or purulent pericarditis. Tamponade with shock is immediately life-threatening and needs emergent decompression.

next_actions: Emergent pericardiocentesis/pericardial drainage with fluid analysis (cell count, Gram stain, culture, hematocrit) and urgent cardiac surgery consultation
Hemodynamic support: IV fluid bolus to preserve preload; avoid positive-pressure ventilation where possible until decompressed
Stat troponin, lactate, CBC, coagulation, type and crossmatch
Coronary angiography/CT if stabilized; TEE to evaluate for abscess/fistula
Continue anti-MRSA therapy; no anticoagulation or thrombolysis

args.rationale: This patient has MRSA bacteremia with infective endocarditis. He developed chest pain, then cardiogenic shock. Echo showed new LV wall-motion abnormalities and tamponade. Pericardiocentesis drained turbid, yellowish fluid. Angiography showed disruption of the prior stent and a rapidly enlarging coronary pseudoaneurysm, most likely an infected (mycotic) stent. This carries a high risk of rupture and ongoing ischemia. Antibiotics or percutaneous treatment alone cannot control it. He needs emergent cardiac surgery: explant the infected stent, repair or exclude the pseudoaneurysm, bypass the affected vessel, debride and wash out the pericardium, and assess the valves and perivalvular tissue for endocarditis complications.
args.followup_or_handoff: Hand off urgently to cardiothoracic surgery and cardiac anesthesia, with interventional cardiology and infectious diseases involved. Keep the pericardial drain in place. Send the pericardial fluid and intraoperative tissue and stent for Gram stain, culture and susceptibilities. Give anti-MRSA IV therapy at kidney-adjusted doses. Give vasopressor or inotropic support and blood products as needed. Do not give thrombolysis or anticoagulation. After surgery, admit to cardiac ICU. Plan TEE, surveillance blood cultures, and prolonged IV antibiotics directed by ID.
